summaries.example: Imagine drawing a picture of a bicycle ride. Put time along the bottom and speed going upward. If the bicycle speeds up evenly, the picture makes a triangle. Oresme used similar pictures to study motion, long before modern science used graphs.
summaries.summary: Nicole Oresme was a fourteenth-century philosopher, mathematician, church leader, translator, and adviser to the French king. He challenged important parts of Aristotle’s natural philosophy. He said a body’s place could be the space it fills, and that time could be the continuing duration of things rather than simply a measure of motion. He studied motion with geometric diagrams, including diagrams that resemble graphs. He also explored infinite collections and proved that the harmonic series does not end at a finite number. Oresme opposed astrology and sought natural explanations for unusual events. In economics, he argued that coinage belongs to the public and warned that weakening money harms a country.
key_ideas: Oresme questioned several ideas connected with Aristotle, especially ideas about place, time, motion, and the heavens.
He described features such as motion and color as ways a substance is, rather than as separate forms.
He used geometry and pictures to study changing speed and other quantities.
He argued against astrology and tried to explain surprising events through natural causes.
He wrote about money and said rulers should not change coins however they wished.
summaries.why_it_matters: Oresme shows that careful questioning can improve ideas even when an older thinker is highly respected. His diagrams helped connect mathematics with the study of motion. His discussions of infinite collections, money, space, and time raise questions that still matter in mathematics, science, and public life. His work also helped develop French scientific and philosophical vocabulary through his translations.

important_terms.definition: A medieval scholar who studied philosophy, science, mathematics, money, and many other subjects.
A feature that belongs to a thing, such as its color, size, place, or motion, but is not the thing itself.
The area filled or occupied by a body. Oresme used this idea instead of Aristotle’s definition of place.
How long things continue to exist. Oresme said time comes from this lasting, not only from motion.
A picture made with lines or shapes to show how much of something there is or how it changes.
Money whose value is lowered because its metal content or weight has been reduced.

questions_to_think_about: Can a drawing help us understand something that changes over time?
Is time possible even when nothing is moving?
Why might people want to test predictions instead of trusting them?
Who should have the right to change the value of a country’s money?

summaries.example: Suppose a car’s speed rises steadily from 0 to 20 meters per second during a ten-second interval. Represent time on a horizontal axis and speed on a vertical axis. The changing speed forms a triangle. Oresme used this kind of geometric configuration to represent nonuniform motion and supported the result now associated with the mean-speed theorem: the distance under uniform acceleration matches the distance traveled at the midpoint speed over the same interval.
summaries.summary: Nicole Oresme was a major fourteenth-century scholastic philosopher whose work connected natural philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, theology, economics, and translation. He criticized several Aristotelian doctrines while often stopping short of adopting the alternatives he considered possible. In his ontology, accidents are distinct from substances but are lower-level conditions or modes rather than separate accidental forms. His account of place identifies it with occupied space, and his account of time derives it from the successive duration of things rather than from motion. His theory of motion describes a successive fluxus that is ontologically a mode of the moving body. Oresme explored an infinite void beyond the cosmos, associated divine immensity with it, and likewise associated eternity with God. In astronomy, he argued that neither Earth’s rest nor a single cosmos could be demonstrated in the usual way, although he retained both positions. He opposed astrology and explained marvels through natural causes. Mathematically, he used geometric configurations to represent changing quantities and motion, proved the divergence of the harmonic series, studied convergent series, and argued that actual infinities are incomparable by the ordinary relations of greater, smaller, and equal. His economic writing defended public control of coinage and analyzed the effects of currency debasement.
key_ideas: Oresme’s condicio theory assigns accidents a status between full substances and mere identifications with substances. Motion, quantity, quality, and being-in-a-place are distinct from substances but not independent accidental forms.

His account of place identifies physical place with occupied space. He also proposed an infinite void beyond the cosmos and associated that immensity with God, while denying space the high status of a substance.

Against Aristotle, Oresme defined time through the successive duration of existing things. He distinguished this from eternity, understood as duration without succession, which he identified with God.
Oresme’s theory of motion treats fluxus as a successive entity added to the moving body and its acquisitions, yet as a mode rather than an accidental form.
He defended the possibility of Earth’s rotation and multiple worlds but ultimately retained a stationary Earth and one cosmos. He attacked astrology on scientific and religious grounds.

His mathematics included coordinate-like diagrams, results about geometric series, the divergence of the harmonic series, and a distinctive argument that actual infinites are incomparable rather than simply larger, smaller, or equal.
summaries.why_it_matters: Oresme illustrates how medieval philosophy could be mathematically inventive and critically engaged with inherited authorities. His treatment of graphs, motion, infinity, space, and time forms part of the longer history leading toward later mathematics and physics, although the source also emphasizes important differences between Oresme and later thinkers such as Newton. His economic analysis connects abstract questions about measurement and value with practical questions about public policy. Studying him also shows that a thinker may argue for the possibility of a hypothesis without finally accepting it.

important_terms.definition: A feature or mode of a substance, such as motion, quantity, quality, or being in a place; Oresme gave such features a lower ontological status than substances.
Oresme’s view that accidents are distinct from substances but are conditions or ways in which substances exist, not separate accidental forms.
For Oresme, the space occupied by a body; this rejects Aristotle’s account of place as the inner boundary of the surrounding body.
A domain associated with location. Oresme treated space as neither substance nor accident and referred to it more naturally with terms such as “here” and “there.”
The successive continuation of things’ existence. Oresme treated this as prior to motion, unlike Aristotle’s definition of time as a measure of motion.
A successive entity accompanying a moving body, while still functioning as a mode or condition rather than a separate accidental form.
A geometric representation using a base and perpendicular lines to display changing quantities, such as velocity over time.
The claim that in a system with two currencies of the same stated denomination but different values, the lower-valued money tends to circulate while the higher-valued money is withheld.

questions_to_think_about: What explanatory advantages might Oresme have seen in treating motion as a mode rather than either a separate form or nothing more than a name?
How does defining time through duration change the question of whether time depends on motion?
Why could a theory allow Earth’s rotation as possible while still affirming that Earth is stationary?
What is the difference between saying two infinite collections are equal and saying that neither is greater or smaller than the other?
Why might control over coinage be treated as a public matter rather than a ruler’s private power?

summaries.example: Think about tracking a runner. Write time across the bottom of a page and speed up the side. A flat line could show constant speed. A slanted line could show the runner speeding up. Oresme used geometric figures in a similar way. He said a steadily changing speed could be shown by a triangle and used such diagrams to reason about distance.
summaries.summary: Nicole Oresme was a fourteenth-century scholar who worked in philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, theology, economics, and translation. Much of his natural philosophy developed through criticism of Aristotle. Oresme did not treat qualities, quantities, motion, and location as ordinary separate forms added to substances. Instead, he described them as lower-level conditions or ways substances exist. He also argued that a body’s place is the space it occupies, not merely the boundary of the body surrounding it. His account of time differed from Aristotle’s: time comes from the successive duration of things, so it is not derived only from motion. Oresme’s theory of motion added a successive flux to the moving body while still treating that flux as a mode rather than a separate form. In astronomy, he defended the possibility of Earth’s daily rotation and of more than one world, but he finally accepted a stationary Earth and one cosmos. He strongly opposed astrology, partly because of concerns about its natural and political effects, and preferred natural explanations for marvels. In mathematics, he represented changing quantities with geometric figures, studied infinite series, and argued that actual infinities cannot simply be ranked as greater, smaller, or equal. His writings on money argued that coinage belongs to the public and warned about currency debasement.
key_ideas: Oresme challenged Aristotle’s definitions of place and time, arguing that place is occupied space and time is the successive duration of things.
His theory of accidents placed them below substances in reality without simply identifying them with substances.
He treated motion as a successive flux that is related to a moving body but is not a separate accidental form.
Oresme argued that Earth’s rotation and many worlds were possible, yet he ultimately defended a stationary Earth and a single cosmos.
He criticized astrology and searched for natural explanations of unusual events and supposed magic.
His mathematical diagrams anticipated coordinate methods, and his work included results about infinite series and infinite collections.
summaries.why_it_matters: Oresme is important because he joined philosophical analysis with mathematical representation and practical economic thinking. His work shows that questioning a famous authority does not always mean rejecting every part of that authority. His ideas about graphs, motion, infinity, and currency belong to the history of concepts later developed in new ways. He also offers a useful example of how scientific claims involve both evidence for possibilities and decisions about which view to accept.

important_terms.definition: A feature of a thing, such as its color, size, location, or movement, rather than the thing’s basic substance.
Oresme’s idea that an accident is a condition or way a substance exists, not a separate form and not identical with the substance.
The space occupied by a body. Oresme used this idea to challenge Aristotle’s account of place.
The surrounding or extended realm in which bodies are located. Oresme said space was real in a limited sense but was neither a substance nor an accident.
The continuing existence of things in succession. Oresme used this to explain time independently of motion.
A geometric picture used to represent how a quantity is spread out or changes, such as speed changing over time.
A series whose terms keep getting smaller in a regular way and whose total approaches a finite value.
Money that has been reduced in value, often by changing its metal content or weight.

questions_to_think_about: What is gained, and what might be lost, when place is defined as the space a body fills?
Can time be independent of motion? What reasons might support each answer?
Why might someone distinguish between showing that an idea is possible and claiming that it is true?
How can a picture or graph become a mathematical argument rather than just an illustration?
Why could changing the value of coins damage an economy?
